what_it_does: Modern AI language models use a mechanism called attention, where every word in a sentence checks its relevance against every other word — a process that grows extremely expensive as sentences get longer. One way to cut that cost is to skip most of the work by ignoring small or zero values, a technique called sparsity (skipping unimportant numbers). Blaze is a specialized chip design that applies this idea at two levels simultaneously: first skipping entire values that are close enough to zero to ignore (value-level sparsity), and second, within each remaining value, processing only the non-zero binary digits one bit at a time (bit-serial computation, meaning the chip handles one binary digit at a time rather than a whole number at once). The key challenge is that these skippable bits are scattered unpredictably across the data, which causes some parts of the chip to be overloaded while others sit idle — a problem called workload imbalance. Blaze addresses this with an Approximate-Computing-Based workload orchestration mechanism that redistributes work across the chip to keep all units busy, and a Leading-Booth mechanism that makes bit-serial processing more efficient. Based on the abstract alone, this appears to be a chip architecture proposal for speeding up attention in language models while reducing power, though exact measured gains are not available here.
